results.summary: The design is a CDMA modulator and demodulator that uses two 5-bit LFSRs to generate Gold codes and spreads a 1-bit input signal. It is tested via a Verilog testbench and intended for lab experiments with an oscilloscope, where an external op-amp simulates channel noise to measure bit-error rate. The circuit recovers the original signal through a receptor output and indicates a valid seed via an LED. The project was created as part of a Latinpractice Bootcamp to study CDMA and Gold sequences.

This is a two-axis position controller that uses 4-bit counters, comparators, and a state machine to move X and Y positions towards user-set targets. The user sets 4-bit target values on the input pins and triggers motion with a button; the current positions are output as 4-bit values for each axis. External hardware includes switches for inputs, a push-button for motion, and LEDs or a logic analyzer for outputs. The design operates at up to 50 MHz and can be reset asynchronously.

This project is a binary-to-7-segment hexadecimal decoder that takes a 4-bit binary input and drives a common-anode 7-segment display. It is tested by connecting a 4-position DIP switch to the inputs and a 7-segment display to the outputs, with appropriate power and resistors. The design outputs active-low segment signals for segments a through g. The documentation is clear but minimal, focusing on basic operation.

This design is an 8-bit synchronous binary counter with asynchronous reset that can count up, count down, or hold based on input pins. It provides binary, hexadecimal, and decimal outputs. It was tested in simulation and briefly on silicon, where the reset polarity was found to be active-high instead of active-low. The design is a straightforward counter and does not require external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout board.

The project is a digital clock that uses time division multiplexing to drive six seven-segment displays with eight outputs. The documentation is essentially non-existent beyond stating that it works and that no external hardware is needed, but switches and LEDs are mentioned. The design appears to accept inputs from switches and drive multiplexed outputs, but the exact functionality is not described. Due to the lack of documentation, details of its operation and testing cannot be determined.

This is a PI-based fan controller that reads a 4-bit ADC value representing temperature and a 4-bit setpoint, then adjusts fan speed via a 25 kHz PWM output with a 20% to 100% duty cycle. It also outputs a signed 4-bit controller value and displays it on a 7-segment display. The design requires external hardware including a 4-bit ADC, a fan, and a 7-segment display. The controller parameters are fixed for simplicity.

Although titled as an SPI master, the documentation for this design describes a simple counter and mirroring function controlled by a 'sel' signal, not an SPI interface. When 'sel' is high, a counter is output; when low, bidirectional pins are mirrored to outputs. The pin names suggest I2C and SPI signals, but the provided description does not match the title, indicating a discrepancy or missing documentation. The design is not tested and its actual functionality is unclear from the text.

This analog design consists of an inverter and a programmable resistor that can connect one of 16 58.218 kΩ resistors between pin ua[0] and ground via analog switches controlled by digital inputs. The inverter uses pins ua[4] and ua[5] and can be used as an amplifier. Testing involves applying signals and measuring currents with an ammeter or oscilloscope. External hardware includes a signal generator and measurement equipment, and the design is intended for experiments with analog building blocks.

This is a 10-bit linear feedback shift register that generates a pseudo-random sequence from a clock and reset input. It was tested on silicon and found to have an inverted reset and incorrect pinout, but worked once the reset was swapped. The design is simple and requires no external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout board. It is useful for applications needing pseudo-random patterns.

This is a simple PAL device that is configured via a shift register, allowing the implementation of custom boolean functions from 8 inputs to 5 outputs. Configuration is done by shifting in a bitstream through a config pin and clock, and an enable pin activates the outputs. It was tested on silicon with various configurations, including a 3-bit state machine, and requires external switches and LEDs for interaction. The design demonstrates a programmable logic device on Tiny Tapeout.
